notes.meaning: Gideon and his men got up early and camped on the high ground beside the spring of Harod, while the Midianite army was camped below them in the valley. The name Harod means "trembling," hinting at the fear that would soon cause many men to leave. Calling Gideon by his other name, Jerubbaal, reminded Israel that Baal could not defend himself.

God told Gideon that his army had too many men for Him to give them the victory. If such a large army won, Israel would brag that they had saved themselves by their own strength. God wanted to reduce their numbers so that everyone would know the rescue came purely from Him.

Following the rule in God's law, Gideon announced that anyone who was afraid could turn back and go home. Looking down at the massive enemy army in the valley, twenty-two thousand men admitted their fear and left. Only ten thousand soldiers remained willing to face the enemy.

Even after so many left, the Lord told Gideon that ten thousand men were still too many. He instructed Gideon to bring them down to the water for another test. There, God Himself would sift through the soldiers and choose who would go into battle.

Gideon brought the men to the water, and the Lord told him to divide them based on how they drank. Most of the men dropped to their knees to drink freely, but three hundred men stayed on their feet and quickly scooped water up to their mouths with their hands. These three hundred stayed alert and ready to move at a moment's notice.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that lapping water like a dog did not test soldierly alertness, but served as a symbolic picture of warriors who would eagerly lap up the enemy's blood.

notes.meaning: The Lord promised Gideon that He would deliver the entire Midianite army using only the three hundred men who lapped the water. All the other thousands of soldiers were dismissed to their homes. Gideon had to rely completely on God's promise to face an overwhelming army with such a tiny group.

The three hundred chosen men took charge of the provisions and rams' horns left behind by the men who were sent home. Gideon sent the rest of the Israelites away to their tents, keeping only this small band above the valley where Midian lay. Now each of Gideon's soldiers was equipped with a horn and supplies for the coming attack.

During the night, the Lord ordered Gideon to get up and go down against the enemy camp. God assured him that He had already handed Midian over into his power. Gideon could move forward in confidence because God's word made the outcome certain.

Knowing Gideon might still be fearful, God graciously gave him a way to find courage before the battle. He told Gideon to take his servant Purah and sneak down to the edge of the Midianite camp to listen to what the soldiers were saying. Gideon obeyed and quietly reached the outposts where the armed guards were stationed.

The Midianites and their allies filled the valley in numbers that seemed like an endless swarm of locusts. Their camels were too many to count, scattered everywhere like sand on a seashore. Humanly speaking, a tiny band of three hundred had no hope against such a vast host.

When Gideon arrived near the camp, he heard a soldier telling a comrade about a strange dream. The man saw a round loaf of barley bread roll down the hill into the camp and smash into a tent so hard that it flipped over and collapsed. Barley bread was the cheap food of poor farmers, picturing how weak and lowly Israel seemed to the nomadic Midianites.

The soldier's friend immediately explained that the bread stood for the sword of Gideon the Israelite. He declared that God had already delivered Midian and the entire camp into Gideon's hands. Hearing an enemy soldier say this showed that God had already filled the opposing army with dread.

Hearing the dream and its explanation, Gideon bowed his head and worshiped the Lord in grateful praise. He returned to the camp of Israel full of bold faith and told his men to rise because God had given them the victory. God's quiet encouragement turned Gideon's fear into confident leadership.

Gideon divided his three hundred men into three separate companies to surround the enemy from several angles. He placed a ram's horn in every man's hand, along with an empty clay jar holding a lit torch. The jars concealed the fire so the men could take up their positions quietly in the dark.

Gideon instructed his men to keep their eyes on him and imitate whatever he did. When his group reached the edge of the camp, all three groups were to act together at the exact same moment. Strict obedience and unified timing were crucial for the plan to succeed.

Gideon ordered that when he and his company blew their horns, every man around the camp should blow his horn and shout the battle cry. They were to call out, "For the Lord and for Gideon!" Gideon added his name not out of pride, but because the dream proved the enemy already panicked at the sound of his name.

Gideon and his hundred men reached the edge of the camp around midnight, right after the guards had changed. The soldiers suddenly blasted their horns and smashed their clay jars against each other. The sudden crash of broken pottery shattered the quiet night and shocked the sleepy camp.

All three companies blew their horns and smashed their jars at once, holding blazing torches in their left hands and horns in their right. They shouted together, "A sword for the Lord and for Gideon!" Holding torches and horns, they had no hands left to hold weapons, showing that God Himself was fighting for them.

The three hundred Israelites held their ground around the perimeter of the camp without charging inside. Surrounded by blaring horns and sudden fire, the Midianites assumed a massive army had broken in among them. Panic swept through the entire camp, and the enemy fled while crying out in terror.

While the three hundred men kept blowing their horns, the Lord caused the Midianites to turn their swords on one another in the dark. In their wild terror and confusion, they mistook their own comrades for attacking enemies. The surviving soldiers fled southward down the Jordan valley past towns like Beth-shittah and Abel-meholah.

Seeing the enemy on the run, the men from the northern tribes of Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh were rallied to join the chase. These were the soldiers who had previously been sent home, but now they gladly stepped in to pursue the routed enemy. They helped make sure the victory was complete.

Gideon sent runners across the hill country of Ephraim, urging that powerful tribe to come down and cut off the enemy's retreat. He told them to guard the streams and the shallow river crossings of the Jordan down to Beth-barah. The Ephraimites answered the call and took control of the waters before the fleeing Midianites could cross over.

The Ephraimites captured two Midianite generals named Oreb and Zeeb, whose names meant "Raven" and "Wolf." They executed Oreb at a large rock and Zeeb at a winepress, giving those landmarks their lasting names. Then they crossed the Jordan River to deliver the heads of the two fallen princes to Gideon.
